To fix StatCheck

What we found

3 possible errors in t-tests or F-tests

Show details

We detected possible errors in test statistics. Note that as the accuracy of statcheck has only been validated for t-tests and F-tests. As Metacheck only uses validated modules, we only provide statcheck results for t tests and F-tests.

Text Recomputed p Sentence
t(1881) = -1.82, p = .034 0.06892 In the actual advice condition, the influence of AI and human advice was statistically equivalent: we can reject source differences larger than 0.048 WOA units, t(1881) = -1.82, p = .034.
t(625) = -1.84, p = .033 0.06624 For AI advice, the influence expected in the hypothetical condition was equivalent to the influence observed in the actual condition at the group level: we can reject mode differences larger than 0.066, t(625) = -1.84, p = .033.
t(636) = 1.42, p = .077 0.15610 For human advice, the test was inconclusive (SESOI = 0.066, t(636) = 1.42, p = .077): expected influence was somewhat higher than actual influence, but this difference was neither significant nor demonstrably absent.

For metascientific research on the validity of statcheck, and it’s usefulness to prevent statistical reporting errors, see:

Nuijten M, van Assen M, Hartgerink C, Epskamp S, Wicherts J (2017). “The validity of the tool "statcheck" in discovering statistical reporting inconsistencies.” doi:10.31234/osf.io/tcxaja. Preprint.

Nuijten M, Wicherts J (2023). “The effectiveness of implementing statcheck in the peer review process to avoid statistical reporting errors.” doi:10.31234/osf.io/bxau9. Preprint.

To fix Exact P-Values

What we found

We found 1 imprecise p value out of 60 detected p values.

Show details

Reporting p values imprecisely (e.g., p < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in p value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., p = .032) unless p values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use p < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., “decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

P-Value Text
ps >= .07 Two features significantly predicted WOA: Flesch-Kincaid grade level, and average sentence length; none of the remaining eight reached significance (all other ps >= .07).

The APA manual states: Report exact p values (e.g., p = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report p values less than .001 as p < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a p value meta-analysis), so report p values with three digits.

American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association.

Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 8 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: editor settings (5), operating system (2), R history (1). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a ._ copy of a .csv for data).

Remove these: Operating system files: macOS adds a __MACOSX folder and a ._ copy of every file it puts in a zip, and .DS_Store files to folders; Windows adds Thumbs.db and desktop.ini. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with zip -r -X, or remove them afterwards with zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store". RStudio session files (.Rproj.user/) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; R history (.Rhistory, .Rapp.history) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; Jupyter checkpoints (.ipynb_checkpoints/) are automatic copies of notebooks; compiled Python files (__pycache__/, .pyc) are recreated when the code runs; open-document lock files (~$...docx, .~lock...#) are left while a document is open; editor backups (file~, .bak, .swp) and temporary files (.tmp, .temp, an interrupted save of R’s workspace, .RDataTmp) are copies a program made by itself.

Keep only on purpose: version control folders (.git, .svn, .hg) hold the project’s history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; editor settings (.idea, .vscode) can hold paths on your own computer. A .gitignore based on GitHub’s templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

To check Power Analysis Check

What we found

We detected 1 potential power analysis.

Show details

We used the LLM model ‘vllm/qwen3-8-27b-fp8’ to check the contents of 2 paragraphs that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses.

Some essential information could not be detected: alpha_level, software

power_type statistical_test sample_size alpha_level power effect_size effect_size_metric software
unknown other 400 NA 0.8 0.07 other NA
text
401 participants completed the survey on prolific.com. Inclusion criteria were being a native English speaker, having an approval rate of at least 95% of previous surveys on the platform, and not having participated in previous studies using similar material. Target sample size (N = 400) was determi…

Cells longer than 300 characters are cut (…).

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 34 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

We found 7 t-tests and/or F-tests where effect sizes are not reported. Check these tests in the table below, and consider adding effect sizes.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 732 columns across 30 data files.

Issues Identified

161 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Qualtrics Survey Metadata

3 of the 30 data files are a Qualtrics survey export. The table below summarises the response metadata Qualtrics records for every survey (not the substantive question columns): how many rows look like previews or unfinished responses that usually need dropping before analysis, the typical completion time (with a count of implausibly fast responses), the data-collection window, and which Qualtrics fields carry personal information to review before sharing. Spreadsheet Formatting

We examined 2 spreadsheet files in the repository; 1 has at least one formatting issue.

File Sheet Issue Detail
advice_coded.xlsx Sheet1 Empty or unnamed columns 1 column is empty or has a blank header.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 30 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

Files are missing from your deposit.

  • 05_run_emfd.py reads emfd_scoring.csv.

The script stops at the line that reads the file.

  1. Find the file on your computer.
  2. Add it to the deposit, in the folder where the script looks for it.
  3. If you cannot share it, for example for privacy reasons, say so in the README, and explain where readers can get it and where to put it.

A script uses a location that exists only on your computer.

  • _inline_csv.py reads h://Meine Ablage//moral advisors//OSF repo//exp 2 - advice taking study//materials//local demo//human_and_GPT_advice.csv.
  • generate_scenario_overview.py reads h://Meine Ablage//moral advisors//OSF repo//exp 2 - advice taking study//materials//local demo//human_and_GPT_advice.csv.

No other computer has that folder, and the file is also not in the deposit.

  1. Add the file to the deposit.
  2. In the script, write the location from the top folder of your project, such as data/survey.csv. In R, here::here(“data”, “survey.csv”) does this for you.
  3. Remove any setwd() lines.

Your code was written for older versions of its packages.

  • llm advice elicitation.ipynb: “AttributeError: module ‘openai’ has no attribute ‘langfuse_auth_check’”

A function or option has changed since you wrote the code, so it stops with today’s version of the package.

  1. In R, run renv::init() in your project and add the renv.lock file this creates to the deposit; in Python, run pip freeze > requirements.txt and add that file.
  2. State your version of R or Python in the README.
  3. Better still, update the code so it also works with current versions.

A script needs a setting from your computer that the deposit does not hold, such as a personal key or the place of data.

  • 03_getting_embeddings.py: “”
  • robustness_scoring.py: “openai.OpenAIError: Missing credentials. Please pass an `api_key`, `workload_identity`, `admin_api_key`, or set the `OPENAI_API_KEY` or `OPENAI_ADMIN_KEY` envir”

We could not check these scripts. Say in the README what each setting is and how readers get it. For an online service, also save the data the script downloads, add it to the deposit, and let the script read the saved copy, as services change or close. For data that cannot be shared, say where and how readers can apply for it.

A script runs longer than our limit of 5 minutes.

  • 02_power-sim.qmd

State in the README how long each script runs. If some steps take hours, save their results (such as fitted models) to files, add those to the deposit, and let the script read them, so readers can check the rest without waiting.

  • 05_run_emfd.py calls os.chdir(), which sets the folder the script runs in. We replaced the call with one that does nothing, so the script ran from the top folder of the project. A folder on your own computer does not exist on another; paths written from the project’s top folder work everywhere.
  • 02_text_analyses.Rmd calls setwd(), which sets the folder the script runs in. We replaced the call with one that does nothing, so the script ran from the top folder of the project. A folder on your own computer does not exist on another; paths written from the project’s top folder work everywhere.

  • 06_text_analyses_mfd.Rmd calls setwd(), which sets the folder the script runs in. We replaced the call with one that does nothing, so the script ran from the top folder of the project.   • eMFDscore_Tutorial.ipynb holds notebook commands that are not Python (%%bash; %%bash; %%bash; %%bash; %%bash; %%bash). We left them out so the code could run; what they install or prepare was not done.

File paths

Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited. The code reads files that are only inside local demo.zip, and no script unpacks it. We unpacked it in its folder before the run. So that others can run the code as deposited, start the code with a line that unpacks it (such as unzip("local demo.zip") in R), or upload the files unpacked.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 17 scripts: 16 ran without error, 0 errored, 1 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

setwd() in the code

3 scripts call setwd(). This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is reproducible only after ignoring a setwd() that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed.

Reproducible after removing setwd(): 06_text_analyses_mfd.Rmd, 02_text_analyses.Rmd, 04_text_analyses_embeddings.Rmd.

> set.seed(1)
> cond <- c("hypothetical","actual")
> src  <- c("human","ai")
> mu   <- matrix(
>   c(0.30, 0.20,   # hypothetical: human, ai
>     0.25, 0.40),  # actual:       human, ai
>   nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
>   dimnames = list(cond, src)
> )
> n_per_cell <- 100
> sd <- 0.10
> dat <- expand.grid(condition = cond, source = src, i = seq_len(n_per_cell))
> dat$WOA <- rnorm(nrow(dat), mean = mapply(function(c,s) mu[c,s], dat$condition, dat$source), sd = sd)
> dat$i <- NULL
> dat$condition <- factor(dat$condition, levels = c("hypothetical","actual"))
> dat$source    <- factor(dat$source,    levels = c("human","ai"))
> raw <- with(dat, tapply(WOA, list(condition, source), mean))
> HH <- raw["hypothetical","human"]
> HA <- raw["hypothetical","ai"]
> AH <- raw["actual","human"]
> AA <- raw["actual","ai"]
> beta_raw <- c(
>   "(Intercept)"              = HH,                     # baseline cell
>   "conditionactual"          = AH - HH,                # (actual - hypothetical) @ human
>   "sourceai"                 = HA - HH,                # (ai - human) @ hypothetical
>   "conditionactual:sourceai" = (AA - HA) - (AH - HH)   # difference-in-differences
> )
> m <- lm(WOA ~ condition * source, data = dat)
> beta_mod <- coef(m)[names(beta_raw)]
> print(round(rbind(raw_contrasts = beta_raw, model_coefs = beta_mod), 6))

> library(TOSTER)
> tost <- function(est, se, df) {
>   sesoi   <- se * (qnorm(0.95) + qnorm(0.90))  # Lakens (2017) Formula 5: z_alpha + z_(beta/2), alpha=.05, power=.80
>   t_lower <- (est - (-sesoi)) / se
>   t_upper <- (est - sesoi) / se
>   p_lower <- pt(t_lower, df, lower.tail = FALSE)  # is the effect significantly > -SESOI?
>   p_upper <- pt(t_upper, df, lower.tail = TRUE)   # is the effect significantly < +SESOI?
>   p_tost  <- max(p_lower, p_upper)
>   ci90    <- est + c(-1, 1) * qt(0.95, df) * se
>   tibble(
>     estimate = est, se = se, df = df, sesoi = sesoi,
>     ci90_low = ci90[1], ci90_high = ci90[2],
>     t_lower = t_lower, p_lower = p_lower,
>     t_upper = t_upper, p_upper = p_upper, p_tost = p_tost
>   )
> }
> m1_act <- lmer(WOA ~ condition * source + (1|id) + (1|scenario_num),
>                data = clean_WOA_strict |> mutate(condition = fct_relevel(condition, "actual")))
> m1_ai  <- lmer(WOA ~ condition * source + (1|id) + (1|scenario_num),
>                data = clean_WOA_strict |> mutate(source = fct_relevel(source, "ai")))

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    scenario_text
1                                                                                                                                   Ella is subletting a room in her apartment to Mia, someone she knows through mutual friends. Initially, they got along well, but over time, Ella has found Mia increasingly annoying. While Mia isn’t doing anything Ella could objectively complain about, her personality, opinions, and interests have started to grate on Ella, making her feel uncomfortable in her own home. Ella knows that finding affordable housing in their area is very difficult and that Mia doesn’t make much money, but she also wants to feel at ease in her living space. Ella wonders if it’s okay to ask Mia to move out.
2                                                                                                                                                                                                             Sophie’s friend recently asked her for feedback on a presentation she gave, but Sophie didn’t think it was very good. At the time, she didn’t want to hurt her friend’s feelings, so she told her it was good. Now her friend is planning to use the same material for a bigger, more important presentation, and Sophie is worried she might embarrass herself. Sophie isn’t sure whether to tell her the truth now or continue to be supportive. She wonders if she should tell her friend that she didn’t like the presentation.
3                                                                                     Laura’s best friend, Emily, is getting married this year and has asked Laura to be her maid of honor. Emily has been with her fiancé, Ryan, for a few years, but Laura believes their relationship is toxic and unlikely to succeed. Emily and Ryan frequently have dramatic fights and have broken up and gotten back together multiple times. Whenever Laura has carefully voiced her concerns, Emily has been dismissive. Laura doesn’t want to let her friend down or damage their relationship, but she feels conflicted about standing as maid of honor for a wedding she doesn’t believe should happen. She wonders if it’s okay to refuse the role.
4                                                                                                                                        Emma, a college student, recently found out that some people she knows have gotten hold of the questions for an upcoming final exam. They shared the questions with her but intentionally kept them from others in their year to avoid raising suspicion with the professor if the entire class performs unusually well. Emma feels that this situation creates an unfair advantage but is hesitant to report it, as doing so might jeopardize her friends’ chances of getting top grades and damage their relationship. She wonders if it’s okay to inform the professor that the exam has been leaked.
5                                                                                                                                                                                                             Sophie’s friend recently asked her for feedback on a presentation she gave, but Sophie didn’t think it was very good. At the time, she didn’t want to hurt her friend’s feelings, so she told her it was good. Now her friend is planning to use the same material for a bigger, more important presentation, and Sophie is worried she might embarrass herself. Sophie isn’t sure whether to tell her the truth now or continue to be supportive. She wonders if she should tell her friend that she didn’t like the presentation.
6                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Nathan recently learned about a job opening that he really wants and feels confident he would be hired for if he applied. However, he knows one person who might be an even better fit: his colleague and friend, Eric. Eric hasn’t heard about the opening yet, and Nathan is tempted not to tell him to avoid hurting his own chances. Nathan also knows that Eric would be very interested in the job if he found out about it. Nathan wonders if it’s okay to keep the opportunity a secret from Eric.
7                                                                                                                                                                                  James is feeling really irritated with his coworker, Alex, who borrowed his favorite coffee mug last week and still hasn’t returned it. Frustrated, James is considering getting back at Alex by starting a rumor that Alex messed up a big project last year. The rumor isn’t true, but James thinks it would make Alex look bad and possibly even get him in trouble. Although James realizes this might be an overreaction, he’s so annoyed that he’s tempted to go through with it. James wonders if it’s okay to spread the rumor to teach Alex a lesson.
8                                                                                                                                                                                                                               Ben’s friend, Tom, has asked him for help with moving house. Ben is completely free on the weekend of the move and would usually not hesitate to say yes. However, he’s noticed that Tom has rarely helped him out in similar situations in the past, often providing reasons for being unavailable. Ben isn’t sure if Tom’s reasons were valid or just excuses, but it’s left him feeling resentful and somewhat exploited. Ben wonders if it’s okay to make up an excuse and decline helping Tom with the move.
9                                                                                                                                        Emma, a college student, recently found out that some people she knows have gotten hold of the questions for an upcoming final exam. They shared the questions with her but intentionally kept them from others in their year to avoid raising suspicion with the professor if the entire class performs unusually well. Emma feels that this situation creates an unfair advantage but is hesitant to report it, as doing so might jeopardize her friends’ chances of getting top grades and damage their relationship. She wonders if it’s okay to inform the professor that the exam has been leaked.
10                                                                                                                 Daniel shares an office with his colleague, Peter, who unfortunately has a very strong body odor. During the winter, Daniel can usually tolerate it, but in the summer, the smell of sweat in their shared office becomes almost unbearable. Daniel has tried several solutions, like keeping the windows wide open and putting up fragrance sticks, but it hasn’t been enough. He doesn’t want to shame or offend Peter and isn’t sure if Peter can even do anything about the smell. However, it’s starting to affect Daniel’s ability to concentrate and get his work done. He wonders if he should talk to Peter about it.
11                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Jake has been looking forward to his best friend Mia’s wedding for months, but he just received a job offer that requires him to relocate on the same day, with no flexibility. The opportunity is a big step forward for Jake’s career, but he feels terrible about missing Mia’s wedding. Jake doesn’t want Mia to think he doesn’t care about her, but he also doesn’t want to pass up the job. He wonders if it’s okay to miss his best friend’s wedding for this career opportunity.
12  Lena’s grandmother is over 90 years old and has been experiencing increasingly severe health complications in recent months. The doctors believe she only has weeks left to live. Lena and her grandmother have always been very close, discussing all the major events and decisions in Lena’s life—except one: Lena and her husband have recently decided to get a divorce. The decision is amicable, and Lena is confident she will be fine, but she knows that sharing this news would deeply upset and worry her grandmother. Lena wants her grandmother to pass away in peace, but not telling her feels like a betrayal of their close relationship. She wonders if it’s okay to keep her divorce a secret from her dying grandmother.
13                                                                                                                                                                                                            Sophie’s friend recently asked her for feedback on a presentation she gave, but Sophie didn’t think it was very good. At the time, she didn’t want to hurt her friend’s feelings, so she told her it was good. Now her friend is planning to use the same material for a bigger, more important presentation, and Sophie is worried she might embarrass herself. Sophie isn’t sure whether to tell her the truth now or continue to be supportive. She wonders if she should tell her friend that she didn’t like the presentation.
14                                                                                                                                                                                                                               Anna has been feeling uneasy about a recent habit: she’s been buying bottled water instead of using her reusable bottle like she used to. She finds bottled water more convenient, especially when she’s busy and on the go. However, Anna is starting to feel guilty about the plastic waste, even though she makes sure to recycle the bottles. She’s wondering if she’s being irresponsible by not sticking with her reusable bottle and whether it’s okay to occasionally buy bottled water for convenience.
15                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Ethan is currently working on a group project where one member isn’t contributing much. To ensure the group gets a good grade, Ethan has been picking up the slack, but it’s becoming increasingly frustrating. He wants to address the issue, but he’s worried about causing conflict or being perceived as a complainer. Ethan wonders if it’s okay to confront the underperforming member.

17                                                                                                                                       Oliver works as a security guard at a supermarket, monitoring the security cameras. For some time, he has noticed an elderly woman stealing small amounts of food and other basic necessities. It seems like she only does this at the end of the month when her paycheck has run out. So far, Oliver hasn’t reported her because it doesn’t feel fair, and the theft isn’t causing significant financial damage to the store. However, Oliver is aware that he could lose his job if his superiors find out he’s been ignoring the theft. He wonders if he should report her behavior to his superiors.
18                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             The other day, Liam was at a store and noticed a customer being incredibly rude to the cashier. The customer was yelling and acting completely unreasonable. Liam felt the urge to step in and say something, but he hesitated, worried about causing a scene or possibly making the situation worse. In the end, he just stood there and watched, but now he feels guilty. Liam wonders if it’s acceptable to stay quiet in situations like this.
19                                                                                                                                   Rachel recently made a mistake at work while entering data into a project report. She accidentally swapped two numbers in a financial summary, slightly misrepresenting the budget allocation. While it’s a minor error that no one has noticed, Rachel worries it could cause confusion during the team’s financial review. She’s debating whether to quietly fix the mistake in the next update or report it to her boss. Rachel doesn’t want to appear incompetent or cause unnecessary alarm, but she also values honesty. She wonders if it’s okay to simply correct the mistake without mentioning it.

1                                                                                                  Ella has every right to feel comfortable and at ease in her own home, as this is fundamental to her well-being and peace of mind. While Mia may not be doing anything objectively wrong, the discord in Ella’s living environment due to personality clashes is legitimate grounds for requesting a change. The purpose of sharing a living space is mutual comfort and harmony, which is currently lacking for Ella. It's important to discuss personal boundaries and space requirements honestly, and sometimes relationships evolve, requiring different arrangements. By choosing to ask Mia to move out, Ella isn't making a personal attack; she is prioritizing her mental peace, which is essential for her daily happiness and functionality. Considering Mia's need for affordable housing, Ella can offer ample notice and support in finding another suitable living situation, ensuring the transition is as smooth as possible. This approach balances Ella's need for peace with consideration for Mia's circumstances, displaying empathy while taking necessary steps to restore her home environment.

In this case, there's an opportunity to fix the harm by giving honest feedback, so you're helping your friend by telling them the truth. Can you really call yourself someone's friend if you prioritise your own feelings of awkwardness about telling the truth over the harm this is going to cause your friend if they don't get honest feedback? Instead of reporting, Oliver might find ways to discreetly assist her or communicate the issue to his superiors to explore solutions, such as community outreach or charitable support, that don't involve punitive measures.
106                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Getting together for tea is what is most important and connecting with friends not whether or not the cookies are store bought or homemade.  If it bothers you make sure to announce where you purchased them from and your friends can then buy them also.  It sounds like you are feeling something beyond just the cookies and perhaps trying to prove yourself worthy of having tea with your friends.  Either way purchasing or making cookies is not the point of the tea, it's to connect and have fun with your friends.
107                                                                                                                                       Emma should consider that Sarah has the right to make an informed decision about her future with Jack. By withholding information about the affair, Emma may inadvertently deprive Sarah of the opportunity to evaluate her relationship and decide whether or not she wishes to proceed with the marriage under these circumstances. While Lily and Jack regret their actions, their remorse does not erase the potential impact the affair could have on Sarah's ability to trust Jack moving forward. Emma's loyalty should prioritize honesty and integrity, particularly when it involves the well-being of a friend like Sarah. Keeping the secret could indirectly allow an uninformed commitment that might lead to deeper hurt and misunderstanding later on. A difficult conversation now could prevent more substantial pain in the future, ensuring that Sarah can make a fully informed choice about her relationship. Emma's decision to speak up demonstrates respect for Sarah's autonomy and right to know important truths before pledging her life to someone.
108                                                                                                                                                                                            Liam should recognize that staying quiet in such situations can be a reasonable choice. Intervening can sometimes escalate conflicts, potentially leading to an even more stressful environment for everyone involved, including the cashier. Additionally, Liam's intervention might not be welcomed or could place him in a confrontational position with the irrational customer. Cashiers often have training in handling difficult customers and may prefer to resolve disputes in their own way or involve store management if necessary. It's also possible that store policies are in place to address these kinds of situations internally, without outside interference. Liam can still support the cashier indirectly, perhaps by expressing kindness or empathy afterwards, or providing feedback to management about customer treatment. Staying quiet doesn't mean being indifferent; it can be a way to avoid contributing to chaos while trusting that the store has mechanisms to manage these incidents.\n

111                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Ethan should avoid confronting the underperforming team member directly, as doing so may lead to unnecessary conflict and tension within the group. Rather than risking a breakdown in group dynamics, Ethan could explore alternative approaches, such as discussing workload distribution with the entire group and seeking collaborative solutions. This approach maintains harmony and encourages a supportive environment, reflecting the collaborative spirit of the project and potentially uncovering any underlying issues without singling anyone out. 115                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Nathan should prioritize integrity and friendship over personal gain by sharing the job opportunity with Eric. Additionally, competition is a natural part of professional growth, and facing it head-on reinforces Nathan's confidence in his own abilities without resorting to deception. In the long run, openness strengthens relationships and creates a more supportive and collaborative environment, which is advantageous for both Nathan and Eric. Sharing the job opportunity reflects positively on Nathan’s character and ensures he makes decisions rooted in fairness and integrity.
116                                                                                                                                                                                                                        It is important for Sophie to be honest with her friend now, even if it means admitting she wasn't truthful before. Constructive criticism can be a vital tool for growth and improvement, and it could prevent her friend from facing embarrassment or failure in a more significant setting. Sophie’s initial intention was to spare her friend’s feelings, but the circumstances have changed, and her honesty could genuinely help her friend enhance her presentation skills. By addressing the issues with kindness and offering specific suggestions for improvement, Sophie demonstrates genuine care and support. This kind of honesty strengthens friendships, as it reflects a desire to see each other succeed and thrive. Sophie should apologize for her previous lack of sincerity and explain her current concerns, emphasizing her willingness to help her friend improve. 117                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         It is acceptable to backtrack on Sophie's word because it will help their friend in the long run. 118                                                                          Mark's decision to continue expressing his concerns is rooted in genuine care for Josh's well-being, making it a morally acceptable choice. As a friend, Mark has a responsibility to look out for Josh, especially when his behavior is potentially harmful to his health. By continuing to voice his concerns, Mark offers Josh an opportunity to reflect on his choices, which Josh might not fully recognize on his own. While it may be uncomfortable, persistence in discussing these issues shows Josh that Mark genuinely cares about him and is invested in his future. Even if Josh initially reacts defensively, this may prompt him to reconsider his actions in a more private moment. Additionally, knowing that someone else is concerned could encourage Josh to seek support or change his habits. Protecting a friendship should not come at the expense of ignoring potential harm; rather, true friendship thrives on honesty and support. Mark should approach these conversations with empathy and patience, emphasizing his concern without judgment, making it more likely they will ultimately strengthen their bond.
119                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                In Rachel's situation, it is reasonable for her to quietly correct the mistake without feeling compelled to inform her boss. The error is minor, has gone unnoticed, and does not impact the overall integrity of the project report. By fixing it in the next update, Rachel proactively ensures the report's accuracy without causing unnecessary alarm or additional scrutiny about her performance. Such minor errors are common and do not reflect incompetence; everyone makes mistakes, and swiftly resolving them demonstrates responsibility and attention to detail. Furthermore, Rachel's decision to quietly correct the issue streamlines the process, preventing distraction and saving her team unnecessary time spent on a trivial matter. As long as she maintains the accuracy and integrity of future reports, doing so in this instance respects the team's workflow while upholding accountability.

126                                                                                                                                  Ella has the right to feel comfortable in her own home, which is a personal space that should foster peace and tranquility. Emma's decision to speak up demonstrates respect for Sarah's autonomy and right to know important truths before pledging her life to someone.

**1. AI | shown 2 times | Mean WOA = 0.000**

Julia should feel perfectly comfortable serving store-bought cookies to her friends. In today's busy world, managing a full-time job and raising children demands a lot of time and energy. It’s important to recognize that convenience is not a moral failing, especially when it allows Julia to spend quality time with her friends without additional stress. Furthermore, enjoying store-bought treats doesn't diminish the authenticity of her hospitality or the enjoyment of their gatherings. Her friends haven't complained because they value the company and the warmth of her home more than whether the cookies are homemade. It's clear that the essence of these gatherings is to connect and share, not to impress with home-baked goods. Julia should give herself grace and let the guilt go, knowing that her intentions—that of welcoming her friends and nurturing her relationships—are what truly matter.

Although James may feel justified in wanting to retaliate, this approach could seriously damage Alex's professional reputation and potentially harm his career over something trivial. Moreover, resorting to deceit compromises James's own integrity and could backfire, damaging his relationships at work and undermining trust with colleagues. Instead, James should communicate directly with Alex, expressing his feelings about the mug in a straightforward manner. Honest dialogue is always preferable to deceptive tactics and helps foster a healthy work environment. Reacting impulsively or out of spite can lead to unnecessary conflict and regrets. By taking the high road and resolving the issue responsibly, James can maintain his professionalism and focus on what truly matters.

During a time when Lena's grandmother may already be overwhelmed with her own health struggles, adding emotional burdens seems unwarranted. Maintaining the peaceful and loving connection they've always shared can be more meaningful than bringing up a potentially upsetting subject. Honoring her grandmother’s tranquility in these final days outweighs the obligation to disclose every detail, especially when Lena's intentions are to protect someone she loves profoundly.

> interaction_test <- function(var) {
>   f_add <- as.formula(paste("WOA ~", var, "+ llm + (1|participant_id) + (1|scenario_num)"))
>   f_int <- as.formula(paste("WOA ~", var, "* llm + (1|participant_id) + (1|scenario_num)"))
> 
>   m_add <- lmer(f_add, data = df_woa, REML = FALSE)
>   m_int <- lmer(f_int, data = df_woa, REML = FALSE)
> 
>   lr    <- anova(m_add, m_int)
>   b_int <- coef(summary(m_int))[paste0(var, ":llm"), "Estimate"]
>   p_int <- coef(summary(m_int))[paste0(var, ":llm"), "Pr(>|t|)"]
>   p_lr  <- lr[2, "Pr(>Chisq)"]
> 
>   tibble(feature = var, b_interaction = b_int, p_interaction = p_int, p_LR = p_lr)
> }
> testable_vars <- setdiff(text_vars, "n_questions")
> interaction_results <- bind_rows(lapply(testable_vars, interaction_test))
> combined_results <- woa_results %>%
>   rename(feature = variable) %>%
>   select(feature, b, SE, CI_low, CI_high, p) %>%
>   left_join(interaction_results %>% select(feature, p_LR),
>             by = "feature") %>%
>   arrange(p) %>%
>   mutate(
>     ci_fmt   = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", CI_low, CI_high),
>     p_fmt    = sapply(p, fmt_p),
>     p_lr_fmt = ifelse(is.na(p_LR), "—", sapply(p_LR, fmt_p))
>   ) %>%
>   select(feature, b, SE, ci_fmt, p_fmt, p_lr_fmt)
> combined_results %>%
>   kable(digits = 2,
>         col.names = c("Feature", "b", "SE", "95% CI", "p", "p (source interaction, LR test)"),

>         test for whether each feature interacts with advice source (n_questions not testable, zero
>         variance in AI advice). b, SE, and 95% CI rounded to 2 decimals; for small-scale
>         variables (e.g., word_count) this rounds some values to 0.00 despite a nonzero effect (see p).")

> woa_b_val <- function(res, var) res$b[res$variable == var]
> woa_p_val <- function(res, var) res$p[res$variable == var]
> woa_test <- function(res, var) {
>   b <- woa_b_val(res, var); p <- woa_p_val(res, var)
>   if (is.na(p)) return("could not be estimated (zero variance)")
>   stars <- ifelse(p < .001, " ***", ifelse(p < .01, " **", ifelse(p < .05, " *", "")))
>   p_fmt <- if (p < .001) "p < .001" else paste0("p = ", formatC(p, digits = 3, format = "f"))
>   paste0("b = ", formatC(b, digits = 3, format = "f"), ", ", p_fmt, stars)
> }
> int_lr_val <- function(var) interaction_results$p_LR[interaction_results$feature == var]

> lr_manual <- function(m_small, m_big, df_diff = 1) {
>   chisq <- 2 * (as.numeric(logLik(m_big)) - as.numeric(logLik(m_small)))
>   p     <- pchisq(chisq, df = df_diff, lower.tail = FALSE)
>   tibble(Chisq = chisq, Df = df_diff, p = p)
> }

</table>> run_lrt <- function(score_col, label) {
> 
>   d <- merged |>
>     mutate(score = if_else(advice_source == "human",
>                            score_original,
>                            .data[[score_col]])) |>
>     filter(!is.na(score), !is.na(scenario_num)) |>
>     mutate(
>       advice_source = factor(advice_source, levels = c("human", "ai")),
>       pro_contra    = factor(pro_contra,    levels = c("pro", "contra"))
>     )
> 
>   m_null <- lmer(score ~ 1                          + (1 | scenario_num), d, REML = FALSE)
>   m_dir  <- lmer(score ~ pro_contra                 + (1 | scenario_num), d, REML = FALSE)
>   m_add  <- lmer(score ~ advice_source + pro_contra + (1 | scenario_num), d, REML = FALSE)
>   m_int  <- lmer(score ~ advice_source * pro_contra + (1 | scenario_num), d, REML = FALSE)
> 
>   # Sequential LRT table (drop the baseline null row which has no chi-sq)
>   lrt_tbl <- anova(m_null, m_dir, m_add, m_int) |>
>     as_tibble(rownames = "model") |>
>     filter(!is.na(Chisq)) |>
>     transmute(
>       Comparison = c("+ direction (pro/contra)",
>                      "+ source (human/AI)",
>                      "+ direction × source"),
>       `χ²(1)`    = round(Chisq, 2),
>       p          = fmt_p(`Pr(>Chisq)`)
>     )
> 
>   # Fixed-effect coefficients from the interaction model
>   coef_tbl <- summary(m_int)$coefficients |>
>     as_tibble(rownames = "Term") |>
>     rename(B = Estimate, SE = `Std. Error`, t = `t value`) |>
>     mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(., 2)))
> 
>   list(label = label, n = nrow(d), lrt = lrt_tbl, coefs = coef_tbl)
> }
> lrt_results <- map2(score_vars, score_labels, run_lrt)
> for (i in seq_along(lrt_results)) {
>   res <- lrt_results[[i]]
> 
>   cat(sprintf("\n### %s  (n = %d)\n\n", res$label, res$n))
> 
>   cat(kbl(res$lrt, format = "html",
>           caption = sprintf("Sequential LRTs — %s scoring", res$label)) |>
>         style_tbl() |>
>         as.character())
> 
>   cat("\n\n**Interaction model fixed effects (m_int):**\n\n")
> 
>   cat(kbl(res$coefs, format = "html") |>
>         style_tbl() |>
>         as.character())
> 
>   cat("\n\n---\n\n")
> }

Python code

This module also assesses whether the paper’s Python code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 12 Python code files.

Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first) and numeric filename prefixes. Python has no source()-equivalent import-based ordering signal (an import loads a module, not the paper’s own analysis flow), so that basis never applies here.

File paths

The data paths in the code to files the repository holds work as deposited, but 7 paths name a file the repository does not hold: moral_advisors_scenarios_third_person.csv, all-sent.csv, single-sent.csv, all-vv.csv, single-vv.csv, mfd2.csv, mfd.csv. The code reads files that are only inside local demo.zip, and no script unpacks it. We unpacked it in its folder before the run. So that others can run the code as deposited, start the code with a line that unpacks it (such as zipfile.ZipFile("local demo.zip").extractall() in Python), or upload the files unpacked.

Files the deposit does not hold

The scripts that did not run through read 7 data files that are not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: moral_advisors_scenarios_third_person.csv, all-sent.csv, single-sent.csv, all-vv.csv, single-vv.csv, mfd2.csv, mfd.csv.

Files not run on their own

6 files are not part of the analysis but of software (a package, its tests or documentation, a tool, a web application), so they were not run or counted as scripts.

scoring.py It is part of the code of the package emfdscore-master, which other files use; it is not a script to run on its own.
init.py It makes its folder a Python package that other files import; it is not a script.
main.py It is part of the code of the package emfdscore-master, which other files use; it is not a script to run on its own.

Execution

The Python code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 6 scripts: 0 ran without error, 6 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 0 are written for Python 2 and not run. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions (e.g. in a requirements.txt).

os.chdir() in the code

1 script calls os.chdir(). This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with pass. Any such script that then ran is reproducible only after ignoring an os.chdir() that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed.

Reported vs. reproduced

103 statistical tests reported in the manuscript text were checked against the extracted analysis output: 67 matched (51 fully, 16 partially) — 65% found.

Some reported values were only found alongside OTHER components after being separated from their own originally-reported neighbours (e.g. a mean split from its own confidence interval). The “Plausible” column marks whether that split is well-supported: TRUE when the pieces still trace back to the same underlying variable (via the output’s own row labels), FALSE when no such link was found — a FALSE match is not necessarily wrong, but is worth checking against its own Source file/Analysis columns before treating it as confirmed.

Self-reproducible output (JASP / jamovi / SPSS Viewer / Jupyter notebook)

2 JASP/jamovi/SPSS-Viewer/notebook files bundle the analyses and their saved results together, so the reported statistics are recoverable from the files itself, with nothing re-run. We extracted 30 result tables (419 individual statistics), typed with the STATO ontology, and export them as a statistical-output JSON document (in the logs) and as queryable rows.

Ethics Approval Check

The paper appears to report data that the authors collected from people or animals, and it has an ethics statement.

We based this on:

In a second study, a new sample of participants completed a Judge-Advisor System task using a subset of these scenarios.

All participants provided informed consent before participation.

For each scenario, participants were randomly assigned to write advice either pro or contra an action that the agent in the scenario was considering (“Write persuasive advice explaining why it is [not] acceptable for Maya to say no to lending Rachel the money”).

Ethics statement:

This set of two studies received ethical approval from the Institutional Review Board of [blinded for peer review], approval number LIP-2024-08, prior to data collection.

How Ethics Approval Check works

This module searches for statements of ethics approval, IRB approval, institutional review board approval, and related terms.

Patterns are designed to capture:

Human research committee names - Institutional Review Board / IRB (US standard), also Internal Review Board - Independent Ethics Committee / IEC (ICH-GCP international clinical trial term); not IEC followed by a number, which is a technical standard - Ethical/Ethics Review Board (generic) - Ethics (Advisory/Review) Committee/Board/Panel/Sub-committee/Commission, in the singular or plural - Research Ethics Committee/Board/Panel (UK/Canada/Australia) - Medical Ethics Committee, Bioethics Committee/Commission, Ethikkommission - Ethical Review Authority/Unit/Office/Agency - Human Subjects/Research Committee / Human Research Ethics (Advisory) Panel - Human Research Protection Office/Program, Office for Human Subjects Protection - Committee for/on the Protection of Human Subjects - Committee(s) on/for (Medical and Health) Research Ethics - Office of Research Ethics - Abbreviations: IEC, REC, REB, ERB, METC, DEC. REC/REB/ERB/DEC are short enough to collide with unrelated jargon (e.g. REC as a recognition-heuristic model abbreviation, DEC as a decision-task label, Reb as an author surname), so these four require an ethics/approval/committee/board/panel/institutional/ protocol word within ~30 characters in the same sentence. IRB and IEC are kept unconstrained as they are not observed to collide in practice. - Dutch: Medisch-ethische toetsingscommissie (METC) - French: Comité d'éthique / Comité d'Ethique

Animal research committee names - Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee / IACUC (US standard) - Any sentence containing animal(s) and committee (or board/panel) within ~5 words of each other — catches Experimental Animal Care and Use Committee, Animal Ethics Committee, Animal Welfare Board, Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body, etc. - UK: Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body / AWERB - Dutch: Dierexperimentencommissie / DEC (see DEC constraint above); Instantie voor Dierenwelzijn / IvD - German: Tierversuchskommission / TvK (advisory committee under §15 Tierschutzgesetz) - French: Comité d'éthique en expérimentation animale / CEEA; Comité d'éthique animale - Spanish: Comité de ética en experimentación animal / CEEA

Approval phrasing - Ethics/Ethical (approval|clearance) [was] (granted|obtained|received|given|secured) - Ethically approved - Approved by the (ethics|irb|institutional|independent|local|review|research) ... - This/The study/protocol/experiment/procedures/methods/research [was] (approved|reviewed) by - Study was ethically approved - (Followed|met|follow) the ethical (guidelines|standards|requirements) - In accordance with ... ethical (guidelines|standards) - Ethics protocol - Approved under (protocol|reference|number)

Waiver / exemption - Ethics/Ethical (waiver|exemption) - IRB (waiver|exemption|exempt) - Exempted from (ethics|irb|institutional review) - Waived by the (ethics|irb|institutional|review) (committee|board) - Deemed exempt - Ethics review that was not needed: Ethics review was not required, did not require further ethical review, exempt from formal human research ethics review, no new institutional ethics review

A template line the authors have not filled in (“[Add ethics approval … here.]”) is not a statement.

Declaration of Helsinki - Declaration of Helsinki / Helsinki Declaration

Patterns are NOT designed to capture: - General ethical considerations or ethical dilemmas in study content - Mentions of “ethics” in theoretical or philosophical contexts - Author approval of a manuscript (e.g. “all authors approved the final version”) - Ethical behaviour as a measured variable (e.g. “ethical decision-making”) - URLs containing “ethics” in path components

When a statement is expected

The module sorts each paper by where its data came from (the internal .data_source(); the signs and how the rule was tested are described in R/data-source.R): - own: the authors collected data from people or animals, for this paper, in an earlier study of their own, or (a protocol) will collect them; - existing_records: records about individual people that the authors obtained for this study, such as hospital records or a cohort; - existing_unclear: existing data about people from a source the module could not identify; - open_resource: an open resource any researcher can use, such as UK Biobank or NHANES; - none: no data about people or animals (a review, simulation, commentary, theory, tutorial, coding of published papers, or figures about groups); - uncertain: the signs were missing or pointed both ways; - no_text: the paper has no text.

A statement is expected for own, existing_records and existing_unclear. A paper without a statement in these classes, or in uncertain, is flagged. The module reads the text, and the results of power, stat_p_exact, stat_check, repo_check, data_check and prereg_check when they ran before it (run it after them); without stat_p_exact, it finds the p-values in the text.

On 199 PsyArXiv and medRxiv preprints labelled after the rule was fixed, the module decided right whether a statement is needed for 86.9% (the earlier live-data search: 83.4%). Its main errors: other people’s studies described in the words of a new study, records and specimens described only as counts, and open resources the paper does not call open.

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Power Analysis Check works

This module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. If specified by the user, it also uses a large language model (LLM) to extract information reported in power analyses, including the statistical test, sample size, alpha level, desired level of power, and magnitude and type of effect size.

The Power Analysis Check module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. Without the use of an LLM, the module uses regular expressions to classify the power analysis as a-priori, sensitivity or post-hoc. With the use of an LLM, it checks if the power analysis is reported with all required information.

The regular expressions can miss power analyses, or fail to classify them correctly. The type of power analysis is often difficult to classify, which can easily be solved by explicitly specifying the type of power analysis as ‘a-priori’, ‘sensitivity’, or ‘post-hoc’. Note that ‘post-hoc’ or ‘observed’ power is rarely useful. The LLM can fail to identify information in the paper, and will not have access to information in paragraphs in the paper other than those that contain the word ‘power’. This package was validated by the Metacheck team on articles in Psychological Science.

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine, Daniel Lakens and Cristian Mesquida

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 128 papers with 246 instances of power statements, 203 were correctly detected (true positives), 22 were missed (false negatives) and 21 were incorrectly detected (false positives). Overall, among all instances flagged as power statements, 90.6% were correct (positive predictive value).

How Preregistration Check works

Retrieve information from preregistrations in a standardised way, and make them easier to check.

The Preregistration Check module identifies preregistrations on the OSF and AsPredicted based on links in the manuscript, retrieves the preregistration text, and organizes the information into a template. The module retrieves text from the OSF with its API, and from AsPredicted with ResearchBox’s API when a ResearchBox key is set (see rbox_token()), or else from the preregistration’s web page. The information in the preregistration is returned. An AsPredicted link that could not be read is named in the report, with the reason.

The module can’t extract information from non-structured preregistration templates (i.e., where the preregistration is uploaded in a single text field) and it can’t retrieve information in preregistrations that are stored as text documents on the OSF.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download information from other preregistration sites, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Marginal Significance works

List all sentences that describe an effect as ‘marginally significant’.

The marginal module searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The list of terms is a subset of those listed in a blog post by Matthew Hankins. The module returns all sentences that match terms describing ‘marginally significant’ results.

Some of the terms identified might not be problematic in some contexts, and there are ways to describe ‘marginal significance’ that are not detected by the module.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 51 papers with 87 statements, this module correctly identified 38 statements (true positives) and incorrectly flagged 22 statements (false positives). It failed to detect 27 statements. Thus, among all statements flagged by the module, 63% were genuine cases (positive predictive value). However, the module missed 42% of all true statements (false negative rate). This validation was made with an earlier, looser pattern; the pattern now requires “significant” or “significance” to follow the trigger word closely (#695).

How StatCheck works

Check consistency of p-values and test statistics

The Statcheck module runs Statcheck. Statcheck searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern, and identifies APA reported statistical tests. More information on the package can be found at https://github.com/cran/statcheck. The module only returns Statcheck results for t-tests and F-tests, as these are the only tests which have been validated, see https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/.

Statcheck was developed by Michèle Nuijten and Sascha Epskamp.

Statcheck considers p = 0.000 an error, as you should report p < 0.001. Furthermore, p < 0.03 is an error if the p-value was 0.031, and one should simply report exact p-values (p = 0.031). When the sentence of a test says it is one-sided (“one-tailed”, “one-sided” or “directional”), a p-value that fits a one-sided test counts as consistent (statcheck’s OneTailedTxt setting; #695). When the paper says anywhere that its tests are one-sided, a p-value that fits a one-sided test in either direction counts as consistent too: half the two-sided p, or 1 minus that half for an effect against the predicted direction. Equivalence tests (TOST) are left out, as their p-values do not test the difference. A statistic written with “<” or “>” is read as a bound, and in a sentence about equal variances an F-test’s two-sided p (twice the one-tailed p) counts as consistent. For more information, see StatCheck.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 685 tests with 34 instances of inconsistent reporting, Statcheck correctly detected 34 of them, and incorrectly identified 26. Therefore 0% of true instances were missed, and 43% of detections were false positives. See https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/ for more details of the validation.

How Exact P-Values works

List any p-values reported with insufficient precision (e.g., p < .05 or p = n.s.), reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000), or impossible (below 0 or above 1, e.g., p = -.22).

This module uses regular expressions to identify p-values. It will flag any values reported as p > ? or p < numbers greater than .001. It will also flag p-values reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000, p = 0.00), which are mathematically impossible — p-values are never exactly zero and should instead be reported as p < .001.

A p-value that is not the result of a test is not flagged: a table note (“* p < .05, ** p < .01”), a figure legend (“Asterisks indicate significant differences (p < .05)”, “Values in bold are significant at p < .05”) or a stated threshold (“p < .05 was considered significant”, “thresholded at p < .001”). GROBID often puts such notes into the running text, so each p-value is judged by the words in its own clause (the text up to a “;” or a full stop), and never left out when a test statistic belongs to it (“F(1, 7) = 8.03, # p < .05”). The column not_a_test of the table says why a p-value was left out (“marker”, “threshold”, “legend” or “named”).

A p-value with the name of a correction or a test after the p (“pFWE < .05”, “padj < 0.05”, “p Wilcoxon = .02”) is flagged only when a test statistic comes before it in its clause (“t(37) = 7.17, p FWE < .05”). Without one it is mostly the rule that decided what was significant (“genes with padj < 0.05 were selected”); such a p-value is “named” in not_a_test. Notes in other forms, such as a marker after the p-value (“p < .05 (*)“), are still flagged.

A p-value below 0 or above 1 is impossible; it is listed apart and not also as imprecise. Often the statistic before it, or its minus sign, was copied into it (“t(134) = -2.32, p = -.13”, “Z = 3.091, P = 3.091”). A value above 1 is listed only after a test statistic in its clause: without one, a “P” above 1 was nearly always another quantity (a proportion, pH, a group’s mean, a model parameter). A number in scientific notation whose power of ten was lost when the PDF was read (“p = 2.4 x 10 -9” read as 2.4) is not listed. A “p” that is the subscript of another symbol (“r p = .64”, “²p = .02” for partial eta squared, “Δp = .33”), or a quantity with a unit, a logarithm or a ratio (“P = 2.9 µm”, “-log10 P = 7.5”, “Ca/P = 1.67”), is not read as a p-value at all (see extract_p_values()). Each p-value has its own row, also when the same one is written twice in a sentence.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (“decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables (as opposed to a table’s footnote text, which the module does see and tries to exclude — see above).

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine and Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: Validated on 226 Psychological Science papers with 5,019 hand-coded p-values, 438 of them imprecise (scienceverse/validation, branch stat_p_exact). Version 0.4.4.3 reported 419 p-values as imprecise, 388 of them correctly (93%), and missed 50 (89% found). Of the misses, 13 are starred table notes (“*p < .05”) that the module leaves out on purpose and 11 are p-values it did not find; of the wrong reports, 20 are p-values the ground truth does not contain (such as “ps < .05”) and 6 use ≤ or ≥. These figures measure agreement with the hand-coding, which has known errors in both directions (scienceverse/validation#48).

How Non-Significant P Value Check works

This module checks for imprecisely reported p values. If p > .05 is detected, it warns for misinterpretations.

The nonsignificant p-value check searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The module identifies all p-values in a manuscript and selects those that are not reported to be smaller than or equal to 0.05. It returns all sentences containing non-significant p-values.

In the future, the Metacheck team aims to incorporate a machine learning classifier to only return sentences likely to contain misinterpretations. If you want to help to improve the module, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

A p-value in a table note (“† p < .10, * p < .05”) or a figure legend (“dashed lines indicate non-significant paths (p > .05)”) is left out, as in stat_p_exact; the column not_a_test says why. A p-value next to words that state a threshold is kept, because such sentences often report a result against that level (“not significant at the conventional threshold (p = .054)”).

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: Validated on three hand-coded sets of papers (scienceverse/validation: 249 Psychological Science, 250 Economics and 250 MDPI papers). Of 1,783 non-significant p-values in the ground truth, version 0.4.4.3 found 1,719 (3.6% missed), and 94.8% of its 1,814 detections were in the ground truth. Some differences come from the ground truth: it lacks p-values with a correction name (“p Bonf = .061”), and counts partial eta squared written with its subscript after it (“η 2 p = .05”), “p = .05”, and some table notes and figure legends (“† p < .10, *p < .05”), which this module leaves out, as non-significant p-values. These figures measure agreement with the hand-coding, which has known errors in both directions (scienceverse/validation#48).

How Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests works

The Effect Size module checks if effect sizes are correctly reported in t-tests and F-tests.

The Effect Size check searches for regular expressions that match typical ways in which effect sizes are reported. It subsequently checks different ways in which Cohen’s d, g, ηp2, and ωp2 can be computed against the reported value. If effects are missing, or might be incorrect, you the module provides a warning. The module was validated on APA reported statistical tests, and might miss effect sizes that were reported in other reporting styles. It was validated by the Metacheck team on papers published in Psychological Science.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 161 papers with 1469 tests, this module correctly detected 1106 reported effect sizes (true positives) and correctly identified 295 cases where no effect size was present (true negatives). However, it missed 23 that were reported (false negatives), and incorrectly identified 45 effect sizes when none were reported (false positives). Among all instances detected by the module, 96% were true cases (positive predictive value). In a validation against 221 reported Cohen’s d effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 218 cases (99%). In a validation against 485 partial eta-squared effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 480 (99%)

How Codebook Check works

This module checks whether the data columns in a repository are documented in a codebook or README. It locates codebook/readme files, extracts the variable definitions they contain, matches those definitions against the data columns extracted by data_check, and reports documentation coverage: how many data columns are documented, and which documented variables are never used.

The Codebook Check module consumes the columns and file classification produced by data_check (and, transitively, repo_check). Files classified as codebook or readme are parsed with parse_codebook(), which reads structured tables (CSV/TSV/Excel with a variable-name column and a label column), embedded labels in haven files (SPSS/Stata/SAS), and plain text from rich-text formats (docx/pdf/rtf/odt). Embedded haven labels from data files are also harvested directly.

Each data column is then matched against the parsed variable definitions with match_column_labels(), using normalised-name matching with experiment-group scoping, haven-label priority, and rule-based label-equivalence merging.

Beyond the variable label, the module harvests the DDI-style per-variable properties a source supplies: the value labels / code list (the 1=“Strongly disagree”…5=“Strongly agree” mapping — from SPSS/Stata value labels and from a codebook “values”/“coding” column), the missing-value scheme (which codes denote missingness, from haven declared missings and labels that read as “refused”/“n/a”), and question text and columns when present. These are carried onto the matched data columns and exported into the Psych-DS variableMeasured (as a schema.org code list plus namespaced metacheck: fields).

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE). When llm_use(TRUE), three optional LLM tiers run: parsing unstructured codebook text that the rules could not handle, fuzzy-matching still-unlabelled columns to still-unmatched codebook variables, and merging conflicting label definitions into a single canonical label.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the codebook_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Repository Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories.

The Repository Check module lists files on the OSF, GitHub, ResearchBox, DSpace (PsychArchives and other legacy- and DSpace 7-based installations), Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare, Dryad, ReShare, 4TU.ResearchData, Mendeley Data, DataONE (Arctic Data Center, KNB, and other member nodes), and LDbase based on links in the manuscript.

A link to a file-sharing service (Google Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive, Box, WeTransfer, MEGA, iCloud Drive, Baidu Netdisk, SURFdrive; see [file_share_links()]) gets a warning and makes the light yellow: such services are not repositories, as files can be changed or deleted at any time, get no DOI, and the link stops working when the account is closed. The report advises a stable repository such as Zenodo instead. Their files are not read, and summary_table$file_share_n counts the links.

Deposits in archives for sequence and expression data (GEO, the INSDC archives BioProject, SRA, ENA and DDBJ, and ArrayExpress; see [seq_archive_links()]), mostly named by accession number, are read for whose deposit they are. The authors’ own are listed with what they hold ([seq_archive_size()]) and are not downloaded or checked as data and code; summary_table$archive_own_n counts them.

R packages on CRAN ([cran_links()], [cran_info()]) are the paper’s own when a paper author is a package author and the paper presents the package; the paper’s own are listed with their version and not checked (summary_table$cran_own_n). A Handle link (hdl.handle.net/...) that leads to a repository read here is checked as a link to that repository ([handle_links()]).

Listing a repository’s files never requires an API key, but some hosts answer faster or more completely with one: OSF allows 100 requests/hour unauthenticated versus 10,000/day with a token (see [osf_pat()]), and Dryad enforces a strict per-IP daily quota on repeated listing (see cache below). Dryad is a special case beyond rate limits: listing a Dryad dataset’s files works without a key, but actually downloading file CONTENTS from Dryad fails with HTTP 401 unless a key is set, even for a fully public dataset (see [dryad_pat()] or [dryad_auth()]). Since this module only lists files and never downloads their contents itself, that limitation applies to data_check and code_check (which do download content), not here – see their own documentation.
