We see no reason to assume this: both require moral evaluation, they differ only in how clear the verdict is. The control scenarios therefore add genuine variance rather than noise. We thus take the correlation across all combinations as the more informative test.

Second, following up on the finding that scenarios with the most extreme initial judgments elicited the least updating in both modes, we tested at the trial level whether the extremity of the initial judgment (|initial judgment -50|) affects WOA in the same way in both modes. We predicted WOA from extremity, mode, and their interaction, with random intercepts for participant and scenario. All coefficients below are expressed per point of extremity. More extreme initial judgments predicted less updating to a similar degree in the actual mode (simple slope b = -0.0052, SE = 0.0005, 95% CI [-0.0062, -0.0042]) and in the hypothetical mode (simple slope b = -0.0062, SE = 0.0005, 95% CI [-0.0071, -0.0052]; Figure 4B). The difference between these slopes, captured by the extremity × mode interaction, was not significant (b = 0.0010, SE = 0.0007, 95% CI [-0.0003, 0.0023], p = .142). When the control scenarios were excluded, extremity still predicted less updating in both modes (actual: b = -0.0047, SE = 0.0006, 95% CI [-0.0058, -0.0035]; hypothetical: b = -0.0058, SE = 0.0006, 95% CI [-0.0069, -0.0048]), and the extremity × mode interaction again was not significant (b = 0.0012, SE = 0.0008, 95% CI [-0.0004, 0.0027], p = .135). Participants in the hypothetical mode thus anticipated less openness to advice in the same situations in which participants in the actual mode were, in fact, less open to it.

Third, a concern with the hypothetical measure is that participants might not forecast their susceptibility for each scenario but instead give a general self-assessment of how open to advice they are, turning hypothetical WOA into an individual-difference measure. To examine this, we decomposed the variance in WOA within each mode into components due to participants, scenarios, and residual trial-to-trial variation.

For each mode, we fitted a model without fixed predictors and with random intercepts for participant and scenario. Scenarios accounted for a similar share of the variance in both modes (actual: 6.7%; hypothetical: 6.9%). Participants, however, accounted for a larger share in the hypothetical mode (36.3%) than in the actual mode (23.5%), with correspondingly less residual variance (hypothetical: 56.8%; actual: 69.8%; Figure 4C). Anticipated influence thus behaved somewhat more like a stable characteristic of the person, whereas actual influence varied more from trial to trial. Part of this difference is expected, however: in the actual mode, each trial involved a different piece of advice, which introduced trial-level variation that has no counterpart in the hypothetical mode.

Fourth, we descriptively compared the shapes of the two distributions (Figure 4D). The means were nearly identical (actual: M = 0.27, SD = 0.32; hypothetical: M = 0.28, SD = 0.27), but actual WOA was more concentrated at the endpoints of the scale. In 37.8% of actual trials, participants did not update at all (WOA = 0), and in 5.1% they fully adopted the advice (WOA = 1). In the hypothetical mode, the corresponding shares were 24.8% and 0.9%, and responses showed an additional peak around the midpoint of the scale (WOA = 0.5). Consistent with this, the median was lower in the actual mode (0.12) than in the hypothetical mode (0.20). Actual updating thus more often took the form of either keeping or abandoning one's initial judgment, whereas anticipated updating more often took intermediate values.

In sum, the two measures converged in some respects but not in others. Anticipated and actual influence were correlated across scenario × source combinations, and both decreased to a similar degree with the extremity of the initial judgment. This suggests that people's expectations about advice influence respond to some of the same features of a situation that drive actual influence. At the same time, anticipated influence was more stable within persons and less often extreme than actual influence. We therefore take the match between the two measures as evidence that people's expectations respond to some of the same situational features that drive actual influence, even though expectations differed by source while actual influence did not. It does not establish that the two measures are fully equivalent, nor that individuals misjudge their own susceptibility to AI or human advice, since expected and actual influence were measured in different participants. Controlling for Advice Extremity: Human advisors gave more extreme numerical recommendations than AI on average (see Figure 1). Because advice extremity could plausibly affect how much participants update toward it (independently of source), this difference could confound the source comparison in the actual advice condition. We tested this by adding advice extremity (measured as absolute distance of scores from the scale midpoint) to a model predicting WOA from source in the actual condition. Extremity significantly improved fit over source alone (χ²(1) = 5.32, p = .021) and independently predicted somewhat greater uptake (b extremity = 0.0018, SE = 0.0008, 95% CI [0.0003, 0.0034], t(911) = 2.31, p = .021). Furthermore, once extremity was controlled, the source effect became significant (b AI = 0.044, SE = 0.021, 95% CI [0.002, 0.085], t(900) = 2.08, p = .038). This suggests the greater extremity of human advice was hiding an AI advantage: When extremity is held constant, people followed AI advice somewhat more than human advice. Given the exploratory, non-preregistered nature of this check, and the number of similar tests run on these data, this result should be treated as preliminary until replicated.

Direct Differences between Initial and Revised Judgments: In addition to calculating WOA, the actual advice condition allows us to also directly compare initial versus revised judgments, without considering how far initial judgment and advisor score were apart. This could be informative because even if people weigh human and AI moral advice equally, the observed differences between human vs. AI moral advice (e.g., AI's observed hesitancy to provide low moral acceptability scores, see Figure 1) could lead to different patterns in overall moral evaluations of scenarios after receiving advice, depending on which advisor people were exposed to. As Figure 5 shows, this was not the case. When arguing pro an action's moral acceptability, both AI and human advisors shifted people's revised judgments up by around 7 points (M diff, human = 6.83, SD diff, human = 15.4; M diff, AI = 7.56, SD diff, AI = 15.8) compared to their initial judgment. When arguing contra, both shifted the revised judgment down by approximately 9 points (M diff, human = -10.30, SD diff, human = 17.9; M diff, AI = -8.18, SD diff, AI = 17.4). Accordingly, change scores were best described by a linear model containing only a fixed effect of advice direction (b pro = 16.64, SE = 0.95, 95% CI [14.78, 18.50], t(1236.32) = 17.53, p < .001), in addition to random intercepts for participant and scenario. Adding a fixed effect of advice source, or an interaction between direction and source, did not improve model fit (χ²(1) = 3.64, p = .057; χ²(2) = 2.66, p = .264, respectively).

We additionally tested whether the magnitude of judgment change differed by direction, using absolute judgment change as the outcome. Contra advice produced larger absolute shifts (M abs, contra = 11.0, SD abs, contra = 16.6) than pro advice (M abs, pro = 8.9, SD abs, pro = 14.7; b pro = -2.67, SE = 0.87, 95% CI [-4.37, -0.97], p = .002)4, and this asymmetry did not differ by source (χ²(2) = 0.73, p = .696, in a model comparison testing whether adding source improves model fit relative to a baseline model with only a main effect of direction in addition to random intercepts for participant and scenario). This asymmetry seems to be explained by a larger discrepancy between initial judgment and advisor score rather than differential weighting of pro and contra advice: People's initial moral judgments skewed positive (M = 60.3, SD = 34.7, see also Figure 5), thereby producing a larger gap between initial judgment and advisor score for contra advice (M = 41.4, SD = 28.3) than pro (M = 30.7, SD = 28.2; b = -11.17, SE = 1.62, 95% CI [-14.34, -8.00], p < .001). A larger gap will yield a larger raw shift under equal proportional uptake, and WOA itself indeed did not differ by direction (M pro = 0.28, SD = 0.32; M contra = 0.26, SD = 0.32; b pro = 0.005, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [-0.03, 0.04], t(902.7) = 0.28, p = .779, in a linear model predicting WOA from direction with random intercepts for participant and scenario). People thus weighted contra and pro advice equally, contra advice simply had more room to move them. Do differences between human and AI advice affect uptake? Human and AI advice differed in their style, their semantic content, and their moral language. Here we ask whether any of these characteristics predicted how much participants updated their judgments (i.e., WOA). To summarize, most of these differences were unrelated to uptake. Among the text features, only linguistic complexity predicted greater uptake, equally for human and AI advice, and sanctity-related language, as well as vice-related language in AI advice, showed weak negative associations with uptake.

To test whether stylistic features of advice predicted uptake, we fit a mixed-effects model (WOA ~ feature + (1|participant) + ( 1|scenario)) separately for each of the ten text features characterized earlier (word count, sentence count, average sentence length, average word length, proportion of long words, type-token ratio, Flesch-Kincaid grade level, proportion of hedging language, proportion of first-person language, number of question marks, see Table 5). Features were modeled individually rather than jointly because several are highly collinear by construction (e.g., Flesch-Kincaid is algebraically derived from sentence and word length) and entering all into a single model produced variance inflation factors up to 29.6, rendering joint coefficients uninterpretable. Two features significantly predicted WOA: Flesch-Kincaid grade level, and average sentence length; none of the remaining eight reached significance (all other ps >= .07). For each feature, we additionally tested whether its association with WOA differed by advice source via a likelihood-ratio test comparing an additive model (feature + source) to one adding a feature × source interaction. None of the testable interactions were significant (question-mark count could not be tested due to zero variance in AI-generated advice). Table 5 reports the model statistics for both analyses for all ten features.

Thus, across advisor types, participants were somewhat more persuaded by linguistically more complex advice. Given that AI-generated advice was more complex, and that complexity positively predicted advice uptake, we explored whether source effects on WOA might be suppressed: if people distrust AI advice, this could be masked by AI's complexity advantage, such that controlling for complexity would reveal lower uptake for AI advice. For each of the two previously significant complexity features (Flesch-Kincaid grade level, average sentence length), we fit a nested model sequence (source only, source + feature, source × feature), testing each step against the previous one via likelihood ratio test. In the source-only model, AI and human advice did not differ in WOA (b AI = 0.021, SE = 0.019, 95% CI [-0.016, 0.057], p = .271). In the additive model, where the source coefficient reflects the source effect holding complexity constant, controlling for Flesch-Kincaid shifted the source coefficient from positive to negative (bAI = -0.007, 95% CI [-0.048, 0.034], p = .738), directionally consistent with suppression but non-significant. Controlling for average sentence length shifted it further positive instead (b AI = 0.028, 95% CI [-0.009, 0.065], p = .140), inconsistent with suppression, but also non-significant. Both features significantly improved fit over this baseline (Flesch-Kincaid: χ²(1) = 8.11, p = .004; average sentence length: χ²(1) = 6.72, p = .010), reflecting the main effects of complexity. Neither feature's interaction with source improved fit further (Flesch-Kincaid: χ²(1) = 0.24, p = .627; average sentence length: χ²(1) = 0.79, p = .373). In sum, there is no evidence that text complexity masks a source effect on advice uptake.

Advisors also differed in the semantic content of their advice, but this too was unrelated to uptake. We tested two measures of semantic distinctiveness. First, in a mixed-effects model predicting WOA from centroid distance (how far an individual text's embedding sits from the average embedding for that scenario, random intercepts for participant and scenario), the effect was non-significant (b centroid distance = -0.106, SE = 0.108, 95% CI [-0.318, 0.106], p = .329), and adding an interaction with advice source did not improve model fit over the additive model (χ²(1) = 0.45, p = .501). Second, we tested mean pairwise distance (how semantically spread out advice texts are within a given scenario and source, a coarser, group-level rather than per-text measure), which also did not predict WOA (b pairwise distance = -0.079, SE = 0.071, 95% CI [-0.217, 0.059], p = .264) and did not interact with source (χ²(1) = 1.99, p = .159). Figure 6 illustrates this dissociation for centroid distance: the left panel shows the different distributions of centroid distance for human and AI advice, while the right panel shows that neither group's regression line on WOA departs meaningfully from zero. How semantically typical or unusual an advice text is, whether at the level of the individual text or the advisor group, appears to be orthogonal to how much participants are persuaded by it. We further tested whether the moral foundations invoked by advice predicted how much participants followed it by entering all five eMFD foundation scores into a single mixed-effects model (Table 6). Four of the five foundations showed no reliable association with WOA; sanctity just reached significance (b = -1.737, SE = 0.867, 95% CI [-3.436, -0.037], p = .046), suggesting more sanctity-related language leads to lower advice uptake. However, given the large number of exploratory tests conducted throughout this section, we do not weight this single marginal result strongly on its own. Adding source as a main effect to this model did not improve fit (χ²(1) = 0.40, p = .527), and letting each foundation's effect vary by source did not improve fit further either (χ²(5) = 5.86, p = .320). Thus, the moral content of advice as captured by these foundation scores does not appear to strongly shape how persuasive participants found it, whether or not the advice came from a human or an AI. We additionally tested virtue and vice orientation the same way as the foundation scores above: entering both jointly, then adding source as a main effect, then as an interaction, with each step tested against the previous one. Adding source as a main effect did not improve fit over the virtue/vice-only model (χ²(1) = 1.31, p = .253), but adding the source interaction did (χ²(2) = 7.54, p = .023), driven specifically by the source × vice term (see Table 7). Simple-slope estimates clarify the pattern: viceladen language was unrelated to uptake for human advice (slope = 1.21, 95% CI [-1.18, 3.60]) but predicted reduced uptake for AI advice (slope = -3.84, 95% CI [-7.37, -0.31]). Virtue orientation showed no comparable asymmetry. This suggests participants penalized morally transgressive framing specifically when it came from an AI, not when the same kind of language came from a human. Again, given the number of exploratory models and p-values examined across this section, this single significant interaction should be interpreted with caution and treated as a candidate for confirmatory follow-up rather than a settled finding.

Further exploratory analyses:

We conducted several additional analyses reported in full in the Supplementary Analyses (available on our OSF repository). First, we tested whether advice was more persuasive when it reinforced rather than challenged participants' existing views (i.e., whether the advisor's stated position fell on the same side of the scale midpoint as the participant's own initial judgment, rather than the opposite side), and whether this depended on source. For human advisors, participants updated further toward the advice when it reinforced their initial leaning than when it challenged it; for AI advisors, updating was similar regardless of whether the advice reinforced or challenged their initial view. Second, outright opinion reversals in reaction to moral advice (initial judgment pro and revised judgment contra, or vice versa) were rare (12.8% of actual-advice trials, 126 of 987), and the overall rate did not differ by source. However, among these reversals, proto-contra flips were more often caused by human advice (68%, n = 38) than AI (32%, n = 18), while contra-to-pro flips were more often caused by AI advice (57%, n = 40) than human (43%, n = 30). Third, WOA varied across scenarios, with advice proving less effective in morally clear-cut cases where initial judgments were more extreme. Fourth, individual difference analyses revealed that participants with more positive attitudes toward AI were more receptive to AI advice when it was actually received, with a similar but non-significant tendency for human advice. In the hypothetical condition, more positive AI attitudes predicted higher expected influence of AI advice but not of human advice, and the two slopes differed significantly. Overall, most participants showed mixed patterns of advice-taking across trials rather than consistently following or ignoring advice.

Taken together, the exploratory analyses support the robustness of some, but not all, of our preregistered results. The equal uptake of human and AI advice in the actual condition held under alternative treatments of excluded trials and in raw judgment changes, and the lower expected influence of AI advice was also stable in size across these treatments. The source × mode interaction, however, depended on how trials with undefined or out-of-range WOA were treated. The correspondence between anticipated and actual influence extended beyond the means, since the two measures were correlated across scenario × source combinations and related similarly to the extremity of initial judgments. It was nonetheless partial, as anticipated influence was more stable within persons and less often extreme than actual influence. Although human and AI advice differed on every dimension examined in the Advice Elicitation study, these differences were largely unrelated to how much participants followed the advice. The few associations we found were small and emerged among many exploratory tests, but they point to concrete hypotheses for future research. First, once advice extremity was controlled, participants followed AI advice somewhat more than human advice. Future research could vary how strongly advice takes a stand, independently of its source, to test whether the tendency of AI toward moderate positions masks an advantage in persuasiveness. Second, linguistically more complex advice was followed more, regardless of source, which suggests that the form of advice may matter alongside its content. Third, vice-laden language reduced uptake only when it came from AI. This raises the question of whether people hold AI advisors to different standards of moral framing than human advisors.

General Discussion

We set out to test whether people expect AI-generated moral advice to shape, alter, or even reverse their moral judgments less than it actually does. This investigation was motivated by a discrepancy that we observed across the existing literature. On the one hand, people often report aversion to relying on AI in the moral domain, expressing discomfort with the idea that algorithmic or machine-generated input should carry any weight in ethical decisions (Aydin & Malle, 2024; Bigman & Gray, 2018; Claessens et al., 2026; Dong et al., 2026; Myers & Everett, 2025; Purcell & Bonnefon, 2023). On the other hand, when people are actually exposed to moral content generated by AI, they tend to evaluate it favourably, often rating it as thoughtful and well-reasoned, sometimes more so than human-authored equivalents (Dillion et al., 2025; Meincke et al., 2026). What is more, studies examining real advice-taking behavior find that AI moral advice shifts people's judgments and behavior just as much as human advice does (Aydin & Malle, 2024; Claessens et al., 2026; Krügel et al., 2022 Krügel et al., , 2023b Krügel et al., , 2026;; Landes et al., 2026; Leib et al., 2024). Taken together, these findings raise a question that neither literature has comprehensively addressed: do people's expectations about the influence of AI moral advice match its actual influence? If people expect to be largely unaffected by AI moral advice while in practice being just as responsive to it as to human advice, this mismatch would have practical implications for how people engage with the AI systems they increasingly encounter in everyday life.

To address this question, we first collected persuasive moral advice on a set of relatable everyday ethical scenarios from both incentivized human writers and GPT-4o. We then had a new sample of participants either revise their moral judgments after receiving this advice, or indicate how much they expected human or AI advice to shift their opinion. This allowed us to compare the actual influence of each source with the influence expected by a separate group of participants. This design extends prior work in several respects. Studies examining algorithm aversion in the moral domain have typically relied on hypothetical scenarios and attitude measures, without exposing participants to actual AI output (Bigman & Gray, 2018; Purcell & Bonnefon, 2023). Studies that do present real AI-generated moral content have mostly asked participants to rate its quality, rather than incorporating it into a judgment task (Dillion et al., 2025; Meincke et al., 2026). And studies that have examined actual advice uptake have generally used advice that was either all AIgenerated or all human-generated, with source merely varied as a label (Aydin & Malle, 2024; Claessens et al., 2026; Krügel et al., 2022 Krügel et al., , 2023b Krügel et al., , 2023a Krügel et al., , 2026;; Landes et al., 2026). Our study expands on previous work by comparing the uptake of genuine longer-form moral advice from both sources, while also measuring how much influence people expect from each.

People are equally influenced by human and AI moral advice

In the actual advice condition of our study, participants were equally influenced by human and AI advice, revising their moral judgments by just under 30% of the distance between their initial position and the advice score, regardless of source (27% for humans, 28% for AI). For context, Bailey et al.'s (2023) meta-analysis of 129 studies using Judge-Advisor-Systems found that people typically revise their estimates by around 32-48% in response to advice, depending on perceived advisor quality. Relative to this estimate, our effect sizes are on the lower end. However, Bailey et al.'s estimate comes from studies using numerical estimation tasks with objectively correct answers (e.g., stock forecasting). When it comes to moral judgment, people may be more reluctant to revise their views to the extent that they perceive morality as subjective. If they do, which is a matter of ongoing empirical investigation (Pölzler & Wright, 2019), they may feel licensed to disregard even advice that is perceived as high quality.

This equal influence of human vs. AI moral advice was observed despite meaningful differences between the advice texts themselves: AI-generated advice was less extreme, longer, linguistically more complex, semantically more uniform, and more virtue-oriented in its moral language than human advice. These differences were largely unrelated to how much participants followed the advice. More linguistically complex advice was followed somewhat more, but equally so for both sources. Controlling for advice extremity did not reveal a penalty for AI advice either; if anything, it revealed a small AI advantage, which we treat as preliminary given the exploratory nature of this analysis. Some of the differences between the advice texts may reflect how LLMs are trained. The virtue orientation of AI advice, along with GPT-4o's reluctance to argue strongly against an action, is consistent with a general tendency toward prosocial, agreeable framing, which may result from aligning models with human preferences during post-training (OpenAI, 2024; Ouyang et al., 2022).

In our hypothetical advice condition, by contrast, participants expected AI advice to influence them less than human advice. Comparing across conditions, the influence expected from AI advice matched, at the group level, the influence it actually had, whereas the influence expected from human advice was somewhat higher than its actual influence, although this difference was neither significant nor demonstrably absent. If actual and hypothetical WOA could be treated as equivalent measures, this pattern would suggest that people tend to estimate the influence of AI moral advice accurately but overestimate the influence of human moral advice. There are reasons, however, not to treat the two measures as fully equivalent: exploratory analyses showed that they converged only partially, varying similarly across scenarios and with the extremity of initial judgments, whereas expected influence was more stable within persons and less extreme. We therefore interpret the crosscondition comparison with caution. The comparison within each condition, where the same measure is applied to both sources, does not depend on this equivalence: human and AI advice were expected to differ in influence, but did not differ in actual influence. Together, these findings suggest that abstract skepticism toward AI in the moral domain may shape people's expectations about AI moral advice, but not how much they are actually influenced by it.

Implications for Moral Cognition and Epistemic Agency

What do these findings mean for moral cognition and epistemic agency as AI becomes an increasingly common source of moral guidance? We begin with the most basic finding: people were moved by moral advice, revising their judgments by around 30% on average. One might ask whether this degree of responsiveness is appropriate. Unlike in advice-taking tasks with objective benchmarks, where it is possible to determine the optimal level of updating, no such standard exists for moral judgment. Our scenarios were deliberately designed to involve competing considerations that reasonable people might weigh differently, and so we can only speculate about what the right level of updating would be.

That said, the observed degree of responsiveness seems neither excessive nor unwarranted. Our scenarios concerned social situations of the kind that people routinely navigate, where the relevant considerations are generally familiar. Unlike stock market forecasting or medical diagnosis, which few people have experience with, moral judgment about social situations is a domain in which people can reasonably consider themselves informed, and there is little ground for assuming that an outside source knows better by default. This is especially true given that our advisors were not framed as expert moral reasoners either: the advice was merely labeled as stemming from "a previous participant" or from "AI (GPT-4)". It thus seems reasonable that people held onto a substantial portion of their initial judgment rather than deferring wholesale.

At the same time, some degree of openness to advice also seems appropriate.

Morality is fundamentally a social endeavour, and remaining open to perspectives other than one's own is arguably often part of what good moral reasoning involves. The advice participants received was moreover substantive, invoking considerations such as social norms, interpersonal obligations, and short-versus long-term consequences, and thus the kind of reasoned argument that warrants engagement. On balance, then, a moderate weight of advice seems like a reasonable response to the materials and task we used.

Next, should people have been moved to the same extent by human and AI moral advice? We detected several differences between the human and AI advice texts used in our study, in terms of extremity, length, linguistic complexity, semantic diversity, and the relative emphasis on virtue versus vice language. However, it is not obvious that any of these differences are morally relevant in the sense of making one source's advice objectively better or more worthy of uptake. We have no principled way of determining whether the AI texts were in any sense superior to the human ones or vice versa. One could imagine a follow-up study in which advice texts from both sources are rated for quality without source labels, which would at least establish whether participants perceive them differently when source information is absent. If AI advice were consistently rated as higher quality under blind conditions, one might argue that participants in our study (where advice source was always disclosed) should have weighted it more heavily. Yet even that inference is contestable: there may be good reasons to be somewhat resistant to AI moral advice even when individual pieces of advice are of high quality, if one has concerns about the nature and legitimacy of AI as a moral interlocutor. On balance, then, the finding that people were equally moved by human and AI advice is not straightforwardly interpretable as either good or bad epistemic practice at this point.

Finally, participants expected less influence from AI than from human advice, although both were equally influential when actually received. This pattern is consistent with a specific concern: that skepticism toward AI in the moral domain leads people to expect less influence from AI advice, relative to human advice, than it actually has. Such a mismatch could matter even if the influence of any single piece of AI advice is modest, since people are increasingly exposed to AI-generated content. At the same time, the cross-condition comparison suggests that this relative underestimation may stem from overestimating the influence of human advice rather than from underestimating the influence of AI advice, since the influence expected from AI advice matched its actual influence at the group level. Yet, our data can show this pattern only at the group level, and our exploratory analyses indicate that expected and actual influence are not fully equivalent. Whether individuals can anticipate the influence of AI moral advice on their own judgments, and whether they engage with such advice deliberately in everyday life, remain open questions for future research.

Limitations

Several features of our design qualify the conclusions we can draw. Because advice mode was manipulated between participants, comparisons between hypothetical and actual influence hold at the group level rather than the individual level. On average, the forecast influence of AI advice closely tracked its actual influence, whereas the forecast influence of human advice was somewhat higher than its actual influence, but we cannot speak to whether any given participant would accurately anticipate the influence of advice on their own judgments. A within-subjects replication with a meaningful time lag between forecasting and advice-taking would be a valuable complement.

Another concern is that actual and hypothetical WOA, though intended to capture the same construct, may not be cognitively equivalent. We followed the procedure of Logg and Schlund (2024), in which actual WOA is derived from trial-level distances between initial judgment, advice, and revised judgment, while hypothetical WOA is elicited as a rating of how much advice could change one's opinion. Our exploratory analyses suggest that the two measures converge only partially: they varied similarly across scenarios and with the extremity of initial judgments, but hypothetical WOA was more stable within persons and less often extreme. In addition, the hypothetical condition relied on self-forecasts, and people are often inaccurate when predicting their own future judgments and reactions. A condition in which participants forecast the influence of advice on others would help disentangle errors specific to selfforecasting from more general lay beliefs about how much advice sways moral judgments. Other approaches also yield a less optimistic picture: Krügel et al. (2023b) found that, when asked retrospectively whether they would have arrived at the same judgment without advice, participants did not appear to recognize the influence the advice had had on them. The divergence raises the possibility that people recognize the potential for advice to sway them in the abstract while having a harder time recognizing, after the fact, that they have been swayed in a particular instance.

Moreover, WOA is undefined when the advice coincides with the participant's initial judgment, so these trials were excluded from our analyses. On such trials, the advice may still have had an effect, for instance by strengthening confidence in an existing view, but WOA cannot capture this. Our conclusion that both sources were equally influential therefore applies only to trials in which the advice differed from the initial judgment. This matters because agreement trials were more frequent for human than for AI advice, so any influence of agreeing advice would not be evenly distributed across sources. Future studies could measure confidence before and after advice to capture this kind of influence, and to test whether it differs by source.

A further caveat is that our comparison between human and AI advice concerns advice as each source naturally produces it, rather than a pure effect of source. Human and AI advice differed systematically in extremity, length, readability, semantic diversity, and moral language. We tested these features as predictors of uptake and found no evidence that they masked a penalty for AI advice; if anything, controlling for extremity revealed a small AI advantage. Unmeasured features of AI advice could, however, still play a role. Relatedly, participants always knew whether the advice came from a human or from an AI. AI advice may exert a different influence when its origin is unknown, in which case an underestimation of its persuasive force could still operate in contexts where AI authorship goes unrecognized. Given the growing prominence of AI-disclosure mandates in policy and platform-governance debates, however, the disclosed-source case is hardly contrived.

In addition, since each piece of advice consisted of a written paragraph together with a numerical acceptability score, we cannot say which component did the work, i.e., whether participants were persuaded by the text or were simply anchoring on the number. These scores were also assigned by the advisors themselves: human writers rated their own advice, and GPT-4o rated each of its texts in a separate step. One indication against pure numerical anchoring is that WOA varied systematically by scenario, with smaller shifts when initial judgments were already extreme (see Supplementary Analyses), suggesting that at least scenario content was being processed (and, by extension, presumably also the content of the accompanying advice). Still, previous research indicates that people also readily follow AI advice without accompanying justifications (Krügel et al., 2026), and that sometimes, adjustment toward advice may reflect simple anchoring (Schultze et al., 2017). Disentangling the contributions of bare numbers and reasoned text, and whether they differ across sources, is therefore a worthwhile avenue for further work, particularly for AI, where it bears on the role of explainability for trust.

Finally, our samples consisted of native English speakers residing predominantly in the United Kingdom or the United States. Culture could shape both which situations count as moral dilemmas and how people resolve them, as well as how open people are to advice in general or to advice from AI in particular. Whether our findings generalize to other cultural contexts therefore remains an open question.

Future Directions

In addition to those already mentioned, several further extensions of the present work seem particularly promising. First, our paradigm captures advice-taking in a stylized, single-shot form: participants read one piece of pre-prepared advice per scenario, in writing, in the context of an online study with no personal stakes. Real engagement with AI moral advisors, by contrast, is increasingly conversational, iterative, and embedded in situations that actually matter to the user. Future studies could examine advice uptake in dynamic exchanges in which users can ask followup questions, push back, or request clarification, and could track moral reasoning across longer time horizons through experience-sampling designs that capture AI use in everyday life. Cases where the moral question concerns the participant's own life, rather than a hypothetical other, would also be valuable, both because personal stakes may change how readily advice is incorporated and because they correspond more closely to the situations in which people actually consult AI for moral guidance. Second, our participants did not choose to receive moral advice: they were simply presented with it. In practice, however, much of the relevant behavior is adviceseeking: people decide whether, when, and from whom to ask. Studying which moral situations prompt people to turn to AI in the first place, and how this compares to seeking advice from human confidants, would complement the present focus on uptake (see Zheng et al., 2026 for work on this issue). Third, an emerging concern in the literature on AI assistants is sycophancy, the tendency of LLMs to align their responses with the views their users already hold (Fanous et al., 2025). Our advisors were instructed to argue pro or contra independently of the participant's initial judgment. Sycophantic AI advice that mirrors and reinforces a user's prior position would presumably yield very different dynamics, and could pose a more serious risk to epistemic agency than advice that pushes back. Investigating how people respond to confirmatory versus disconfirmatory AI moral advice, and whether they can detect sycophantic patterns over repeated interactions, is an important next step. Fourth, our studies measured how much people expected to be influenced by advice, but not whether they are aware of being influenced, or how they reflect on their own preferences for human versus AI advice. Studying such awareness directly, for instance by combining advice-taking tasks with retrospective reports of influence, would clarify whether people can track the influence of AI moral advice on their own judgments.

Conclusion

As AI systems become routine participants in everyday moral discourse, understanding how people engage with their advice is important. Prior work on AI moral advice uptake has largely manipulated source as a label while holding content constant, so it remains unclear how people respond to genuine differences between human-and AI-generated advice, and whether they anticipate that response. Our study addresses both questions by eliciting real moral advice from incentivized human writers and GPT-4o, and comparing its actual influence with forecasts of its influence from an independent sample.

The picture that emerges is nuanced. People updated their moral judgments in response to AI-generated advice to the same extent as they did in response to human advice, yet a separate group expected AI advice to influence them less than human advice. Abstract skepticism toward AI may thus shape expectations about its influence, even when it does not reduce its actual influence, at least when authorship is disclosed. At the group level, this relative underestimation may reflect an overestimation of the influence of human advice rather than an underestimation of the influence of AI advice. Whether individuals can anticipate the influence of AI moral advice on their own judgments, and engage deliberately with AI moral input in practice, is in our view the question most worth pursuing next.
